kaigo-atomic-brain-lobes.heading: Four cerebral lobes and cognition
paragraphs: The cerebrum is described in four lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital. Frontal functions include planning actions, thinking, movement, emotion and motivation. Parietal functions include integrating sensations and understanding bodily and object positions in space. Connect names and main functions with everyday use.

The temporal lobe contributes to understanding sound, language and memory. The occipital lobe processes visual information. Understanding spoken meaning and recognizing what is seen both matter in daily life; distinguish their main roles.

The source diagram also associates the frontal lobe with smell, emotion, motivation and will, and the parietal lobe with taste, understanding and judgment. It summarizes main functions rather than locating every aspect of one sense or action exclusively in that lobe. Do not use labels as a one-to-one diagnostic chart.

Cognition includes learning and remembering, understanding and using language, recognizing objects, acting, planning and sequencing. Several functions contribute to one situation. Difficulty with one action does not establish identical loss of all cognition.

[Learning example] Someone who struggles with sequencing may recognize familiar faces. Check abilities and which stage needs support rather than focusing only on limitations. This example does not identify an impaired lobe or disease.

Dementia involves reduced cognition affecting daily or social life and has various causes. Do not diagnose it from one memory lapse or dismiss new difficulties as age alone. Record the person’s own words and changes and arrange appropriate assessment.

This lesson teaches region names, main functions and perspectives for support. Professionals perform actual diagnosis and functional assessment. Care follows condition, the individual care plan and facility instruction.

kaigo-atomic-forgetting.heading: Do not turn a forgetting comparison table into personal diagnosis
paragraphs: When comparing age-related forgetting with dementia-related forgetting, consider whether part or all of an event is forgotten, the course, personal awareness and daily-life effects. Comparisons guide what to check.

Do not apply table tendencies without exception. People with dementia may notice forgetting and feel anxious. Awareness does not rule out dementia. Professional assessment considers the course and everyday functioning too.
The degree and course of forgetting vary by underlying illness and condition. Lack of awareness alone does not diagnose dementia, and change does not proceed at one speed for everyone.
Respect life history, routines, remaining abilities and motivation. Speak briefly and clearly and allow response time. Do not rearrange rooms or familiar items solely for staff convenience.
Consider shared activity and daily rhythms according to wishes and condition. Ask what worries the person and discuss support for feeling secure. Do not force identical activities on everyone.

Acknowledging emotion differs from declaring an unconfirmed event true. Do not argue for an admission of error or publicly test memory and cause embarrassment. Preserve the person’s own words, check facts together if needed and tell the person responsible. Actual support follows individual assessment, the care plan and facility instruction.

kaigo-atomic-dementia-types.heading: Main causes of dementia and individual differences
paragraphs: Alzheimer’s dementia can involve brain atrophy, difficulty remembering new events and gradual functional change. Vascular dementia relates to cerebrovascular damage; abilities and difficulties vary by affected areas. Changes may be stepwise and may accompany hemiplegia or aphasia.

Dementia with Lewy bodies may involve visual hallucinations, fluctuations in cognition, attention or responsiveness, and Parkinsonian symptoms such as slowed movement or stiffness. Specifically record when and how these appear.

REM sleep behavior disorder, with vocalizing or moving in response to dream content, can also be associated with dementia with Lewy bodies. Understanding ordinary REM sleep differs from assessing actual sleep behavior. Record actions and times and consult healthcare professionals without diagnosing from this feature alone.

Dementia with Lewy bodies involves abnormal accumulation of the protein alpha-synuclein. Do not reinterpret the diagram as a disease consisting only of occipital-lobe atrophy. Cognition, movement, sleep and other aspects require professional assessment.

Frontotemporal dementia can involve frontal or temporal atrophy and prominent changes in behavior, personality or language, including repeated actions. Symptoms vary, and not every feature is present in everyone.

Do not assume personality from diagnosis, such as always cheerful in Alzheimer’s or always aggressive in frontotemporal dementia. Brain atrophy alone does not explain the entire cause or functional picture. Check the person individually.

Some medicines for Alzheimer’s dementia aim to slow progression. Treatment aims, effects and responses vary. Do not promise every medicine slows every dementia type; physicians decide medication. Care workers communicate changes and difficulties and follow the person’s plan.

kaigo-atomic-dementia-symptoms.heading: Core symptoms, BPSD and their context
paragraphs: Core symptoms include difficulty learning new information, disorientation about time, place or people, impaired sequencing and executive function, and difficulties with understanding or judgment. Beyond memorizing labels, identify effects on specific daily activities.

[Example for understanding] Sequencing difficulty can affect cooking, while judgment difficulty can affect money handling. The same diagnosis does not mean every difficulty appears to the same degree in everyone.

Behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) include anxiety, irritability, hallucinations, delusions, restlessness and repeated walking. Disease and cognitive difficulty can interact with bodily condition, surroundings, relationships and feelings. BPSD are also called peripheral symptoms, but this does not mean they matter less than core symptoms.

Harsh words or striking out may relate to fear of not knowing what will happen, pain or difficulty communicating toileting needs. Do not end with an aggressive-personality label. Observe the actual action and surrounding events and check the person’s difficulties.

Walking may have a purpose. For example, moving about before meals is not automatically meaningless wandering. Consider the person’s own words and context, such as looking for something or needing the toilet. This learning example does not justify deciding the purpose before asking.

Core symptoms and BPSD categories organize observation perspectives, not importance rankings. Do not blame everything on surroundings or personality; share bodily changes with the team too. Symptom names do not authorize staff to increase medication or restrict behavior.

Ask about the person’s anxiety and needs. Tell the person responsible what changes you observed, clearly distinguishing them from what is still unconfirmed. Provide support according to individual assessment and the care plan. If an urgent abnormality occurs, seek the necessary help instead of continuing routine questions.

kaigo-atomic-urination-volume.heading: Understand urine pathways and the urge to urinate
paragraphs: The kidneys produce urine by removing waste and excess water from blood. Ureters carry it to the bladder, which stores urine temporarily rather than producing it. During urination, it leaves through the urethra.
The renal pelvis is the collecting region within a kidney that connects to the ureter. Ureters carry urine to the bladder; the urethra carries it out. Similar names describe different connections.

The cerebrum, brainstem, spinal cord and other neural functions help regulate storage and passing urine. Feeling the urge, finding the toilet and reaching it are distinct abilities; check support needed for each.
The source gives approximately 500 mL bladder capacity and an urge around 200–300 mL as learning guides, not fixed volumes felt by every person. Never use unknown volume to deny access to the toilet.
The male urethra is generally longer, with the prostate surrounding part of it. Structural differences do not establish mobility or assistance wishes.

When the person says they want to urinate, acknowledge their wish and current condition and support them using an individualized method. Do not use general bladder-capacity figures as a reason to make them hold their urine or as a basis for diagnosing disease. Report changes to the person responsible.

kaigo-atomic-urine-reference.heading: Read urine/stool amounts, frequencies and colors with conditions
paragraphs: The source urine table gives a daily reference amount of 1,000–1,500 mL, with large examples of 2,000–3,000 mL or more and small examples of 300–500 mL or less. Preserve the one-day period. These learning guides do not diagnose everyone by identical numbers. Polyuria means a large amount and oliguria a small amount, but terms or source numbers alone do not diagnose an individual.

The frequency table gives examples of four to six daily episodes and attention guides of eight or more daytime and two or more nighttime episodes. Frequency and total volume differ. Unknown amounts per episode cannot become a daily total from frequency alone.

Interpret urine volume together with the collection period, fluid intake from food and drinks, medication, illness, climate and other relevant conditions. For example, do not compare 600 mL collected over half a day directly with a full-day reference value, or double it by inventing an unmeasured amount for the rest of the day. Check the person’s usual condition and the circumstances needed for assessment by healthcare professionals.
Pale yellow to clear is the table’s usual urine-color example. Record and report cloudiness, redness, dark brown and other changes as observed. Color alone does not establish the disease causing it.

The table describes usual urine as odorless and contrasts strong ammonia odor. In practice, record which urine was observed and under what conditions. Strong odor alone does not establish infection or another cause; report it with other changes and personal concerns.

The stool table gives one or two daily episodes and brown color as usual examples. Frequency, form, amount and color vary with food, illness and personal patterns. Compare with the individual baseline rather than judging solely by a table mismatch.

Specifically record red, black or whitish stool and report according to condition. Food, medication and illness can influence appearance; observed color alone does not establish bleeding or another cause.

With unusual changes or distress, do not delay necessary contact to finish records. Follow the individual observation/reporting plan and do not independently change fluids or medication from general numbers alone.

kaigo-atomic-diaper-fit.heading: Diaper changing: cleanliness, fit and checks afterward
paragraphs: Before changing the diaper, check the person’s physical condition, explain the purpose and what you will do, and obtain consent. Protect privacy with curtains or similar measures. Before starting, prepare the necessary supplies, adjust the bed to a suitable working height and prepare a waterproof sheet. Avoid leaving the person’s body exposed for a long time.

Use side-lying, lying on the back or hip lifting only when appropriate to ability, condition and the individual care plan. Do not assume everyone can copy the illustration; check methods with pain or movement difficulty. The source example inserts waterproof material in side-lying, returns to lying on the back, lowers pants while an able person lifts their hips, then opens diaper tapes. Check whether actions are possible and permitted; do not force hip lifting or position changes.

Check genital-washing water for suitable warmth. The source uses a shower bottle, but equipment and washing follow facility methods suited to the person. Attend to folds, avoid rubbing and gently dry afterward. In the female example, wash from urethral side toward anus. Do not return anal contamination toward the urethra; use a clean surface or material for every wipe.

Fold the dirty diaper’s contaminated surface inward for disposal. Separate clean and used items and avoid contaminating a new diaper or clean area with the dirty diaper or gloves. At dirty-to-clean transitions, remove gloves, perform hand hygiene and use fresh gloves if needed under facility procedures. The source combines position changes with removing the old diaper. Follow a confirmed method for suitable turning, including returning to the back, and arrangements that protect clean items.

The changing illustrations simplify steps for learning. Apparent overlap between dirty and new diapers does not permit contaminating clean items. Actual changing uses trained methods maintaining clean–dirty boundaries.

The source gives a two- or three-finger-space example at abdomen and thighs to explain avoiding tightness. It is not a universal measurement for every product. Check actual type, size and instructions with skin condition and personal sensation.

No leak does not complete support if rolled edges, wrinkles or tightness cause pain. Wrinkle-related pressure can injure skin. Follow product instructions to check position and wrinkles, skin, sensations, clothing and sheets. Tell the person responsible about abnormalities or pain. The source also gives tightness-related itching as an example; check reported symptoms and skin without independently deciding tightness or another cause.

When replacing clothing, the example lets able people perform permitted actions such as lifting hips. Do not demand difficult movements; match support to abilities and wishes. Finish by checking condition and comfort, restoring safe bed and surroundings, tidying supplies and performing necessary hand hygiene. Ventilate without chilling the person. Reading this explanation does not establish practical competence; follow the individual care plan and facility procedures and training.

92.title: Four cerebral lobes and cognition
objectives: Explain main lobe functions without fixed one-to-one mapping.
Separate cognitive abilities from the specific parts needing support.
92.context: Learn brain regions and connect them with everyday cognition, without diagnosing from names.
92.artCaption: Staff explain using a brain model. The model alone does not establish personal functions or diagnosis.

93.title: Do not turn a forgetting comparison table into personal diagnosis
objectives: Distinguish comparison-table tendencies from individual diagnosis.
Use concerns, life history and remaining abilities in support.
93.context: Listen to concerns about forgetting and consider table conditions and individual differences. Awareness alone does not establish disease status.
93.artCaption: The person and worker discuss written materials. The image alone does not establish dementia status or confirmed plans.

94.title: Main causes of dementia and individual differences
objectives: Explain features of major causes and individual differences.
Communicate observed symptoms without diagnosing from one feature.
94.context: Organize features of main underlying diseases without using names for personality assumptions or independent medication decisions.
94.artCaption: Staff check information with documents. This does not identify the background person’s diagnosis or dementia type.

95.title: Core symptoms, BPSD and their context
objectives: Distinguish core and behavioral/psychological symptoms and consider context.
Specifically report the person’s own words and circumstances before and after actions.
95.context: Learn to check personal difficulties beyond memorizing symptom names, without assuming causes from example behavior.
95.artCaption: The person speaks to staff. A hand on the chest alone does not establish disease or causes of behavior.

96.title: Understand urine pathways and the urge to urinate
objectives: Explain the route from urine production to leaving the body.
Distinguish capacity guides from personal urge and individual support.
96.context: Study urination and source values, not a reason to make someone wait until numbers are checked.
96.artCaption: A bladder model helps explain mechanisms. The image does not measure personal urine volume or bladder capacity.

97.title: Read urine/stool amounts, frequencies and colors with conditions
objectives: Distinguish daily amounts and frequencies from observation-period conditions.
Report urine/stool changes separately from assumed causes.
97.context: Read tables with units, periods and differences from usual, without diagnosing from numbers or colors alone.
97.artCaption: Staff compare records, checking observation duration and conditions as well as amount.

98.title: Diaper changing: cleanliness, fit and checks afterward
objectives: Explain clean–dirty boundaries and personal comfort during changing.
Check fit through product instructions, skin and personal sensation together.
98.context: Learn checks before, during and after changing. Reading an explanation does not establish practical competence.
98.artCaption: Staff prepare by checking instructions and supplies. The image proves neither completed changing nor correct fit.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-brain-lobes.prompt: Which approach to support is appropriate?
options: Recognizing faces means no sequencing support is needed.
Sequencing difficulty means all cognition is lost.
Separate abilities from difficulties and support the necessary stage.
One action establishes the impaired lobe and disease.
rationales: Face recognition and sequencing differ; recognition does not prove no help is needed.
Difficulty in one function does not establish loss of all functions.
This checks remaining abilities and specific support needs.
One action cannot establish an affected region or disease.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-brain-lobes.reading: [Learning example] The person struggles to organize task order but recognizes familiar staff faces.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-forgetting.prompt: Which understanding is appropriate at this point?
options: Awareness of forgetting alone cannot rule out dementia.
Awareness establishes absence of dementia.
Expressing worry establishes dementia.
Older age removes the need to check daily-life changes.
rationales: Some people with dementia have awareness; assessment also considers course and daily-life effects.
This applies a comparison-table tendency without exceptions.
Worry alone does not diagnose dementia.
Do not overlook new changes because of age; arrange necessary checks.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-forgetting.reading: [Learning example] The person says, ‘I’ve been forgetting things lately, and I’m worried.’ Staff have not checked changes in daily life yet.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-dementia-types.prompt: How should this record be handled?
options: Mention of REM means everyone has dementia with Lewy bodies.
Sleep information need not be shared for dementia assessment.
One record confirms dementia with Lewy bodies.
Separate ordinary REM knowledge from actual behavior and tell healthcare professionals the observations.
rationales: REM occurs in ordinary sleep; the word alone does not establish disease.
REM sleep behavior disorder can be related, and specific actions can inform assessment.
Diagnosis needs professional assessment across several aspects.
This distinguishes concepts from observed facts and communicates assessment information.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-dementia-types.reading: [Learning example] After learning about REM, a worker reads a record of sleep vocalizations and limb movements appearing to follow dreams.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-dementia-sympto.prompt: Which initial understanding and response are appropriate?
options: Walking is always meaningless, so do not ask why.
Speak to the person and check circumstances, such as what they are seeking.
Independently increase medication based only on pacing.
Assume preventing movement also establishes the cause.
rationales: Walking may have a purpose or reflect difficulty; do not call it meaningless.
Check the person’s own words and surrounding events without assuming the background.
Staff cannot independently change medication based only on behavior.
Stopping movement does not identify cause. Symptom names do not justify restraint.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-dementia-sympto.reading: [Learning example] Before a meal, the person walks back and forth in the corridor. Staff have not asked the reason yet.

options: Acknowledge the urge and support according to condition and the individual care plan.
Do not accept the request until at least 200 mL is confirmed.
Make the 500 mL example everyone’s required waiting volume.
An urge means identical volumes and causes in everyone.
rationales: These are learning reference values, not rules for ignoring the urge and needed help.
Measuring a general reference must not become a condition for starting support.
The capacity example is not a universal holding target.
An urge alone does not establish actual volume or cause.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-urination-volum.reading: [Learning example] The person says they want to use the toilet. The worker does not know current bladder volume.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-urine-reference.prompt: What can appropriately be said from this record?
options: Compare 600 mL directly with a full-day table.
Doubling guarantees 1,200 mL as the measured daily amount.
Preserve the half-day condition and distinguish it from an actual daily measurement.
Record volume without collection duration.
rationales: Half-day and full-day observation periods differ and cannot be treated as identical.
Doubling an invented unmeasured remainder does not produce a measured value.
Preserving period and units accurately communicates what was actually established.
Observation duration is necessary for interpreting volume.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-urine-reference.reading: [Learning example] 600 mL was measured over half a day. No measurement exists for the remaining time. The source gives daily reference values.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-diaper-fit.prompt: Which check is appropriate before considering support complete?
options: No leak removes the need to check pain.
Follow product instructions to check position, wrinkles, skin and personal sensation and discuss needed action.
Space for fingers removes consideration of product type or pain.
Finish arranging clean items in dirty gloves.
rationales: Leak status alone does not establish fit or comfort.
Check rolled edges and pain and respond according to the product and individual condition.
The finger example does not establish every product’s fit or rule out pain.
Dirty-to-clean work needs appropriate glove changes and hand hygiene.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-diaper-fit.reading: [Learning example] After changing, there is no leak, but the diaper edge is rolled inward and the person reports pain.
